migrate

MY-grayt -- built on the Latin root for 'to move.' · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To migrate is to move from one region, habitat, or country to another, often seasonally or permanently.

Each winter, entire flocks of geese migrate south along the same ancient route.

Example

Every autumn, herds of wildebeest migrate hundreds of miles across the plains of East Africa, following the rains to reach fresh grazing land before circling back the following year.

That large-scale seasonal journey to a new habitat, often repeated year after year, is what it means to migrate. Unlike 'wander,' which can be aimless, migrate implies a purposeful, often instinctual journey.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

journey: To journey is simply to travel a long distance, with no pattern implied. To migrate is more specific: a purposeful move from one region or habitat to another, often seasonal and repeated. A hiker can journey once; geese migrate along the same route every year.

emigrate: To emigrate is to leave your own country and settle permanently in another -- a one-way move made by people. To migrate is broader: animals, people, or whole populations moving between regions, often seasonally and often with a return trip built in.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

remain: to stay in the same place

settle: to establish a permanent home in one place

Where it sits · how large and lasting the move is — relocate → migrate → resettle

relocate vs. migrate: Relocate is a more general, everyday word than migrate -- relocate can describe a single move by one person or company, while migrate often implies a larger, seasonal, or instinctual movement, especially of animals or populations.

resettle vs. migrate: Resettle can feel more permanent than migrate: migrate often implies a movement that may repeat seasonally, while resettle suggests establishing a new, lasting home.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — migr-

root — migr-: to move, to wander (Latin (migrare))

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: to make or do; forms a verb (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin migrare meant 'to move from one place to another,' and the suffix -ate marks it as a verb. To migrate is simply that act of relocating -- geese flying south, or people moving to a new country.

Use the root in a new word: emigrate

Use the root in a new word: emigrate: Her grandparents emigrated in 1952, two years before her mother was born.
